# R Markdown

## Overview

R Markdown is a typesetting framework that allows you to combine code, text, and mathematical symbols in a single document. This whole document was written in R Markdown. R Markdown documents have the file extension .Rmd.

We recommend using [RStudio](https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/) to edit R and R Markdown scripts.
To create an R Markdown document, go to `File -> New File -> R Markdown`. You can also copy this file and use it as a template (recommended).

You can render, or **knit**, an R Markdown file to a .pdf or .html file by clicking the `Knit` button in the bar under the file name. You will probably need to install either [TinyTex](https://yihui.org/tinytex/), [MacTex](https://www.tug.org/mactex/) (Mac only), or [MikTex](https://miktex.org) (any operating system) in order for this to work properly.

Code is written in **code chunks** (Section 4.2). Texts are formatted using **Markdown** syntax (Section 4.3).

## Code chunks

You can easily intersperse text and code. The gray chunks you see are called **code chunks**. To insert a code chunk at the location of your cursor, click `Code -> Insert Chunk`. Alternatively, you can use a keyboard shortcut: `Ctrl + Alt + I` for Windows or `Cmd + Option + I` for Mac.

Let's practice:

*(place a code chunk here)*

Here are some helpful **options** (and their default settings) to control if and how code chunks are displayed when the document is rendered:

- `echo = TRUE`: display the chunk's code in addition to its output
- `eval = TRUE`: run the chunk when rendering the document
- `include = TRUE`: display the chunk's code when rendering the document
- `message = TRUE`: display code messages when rendering the document
- `warning = TRUE`: display code warnings when rendering the document
- `fig.align`: e.g., `fig.align = "center"`
- `out.width`: e.g., `out.width = "75%"`

You can also name a code chunk. The example below is name ``code chunk options".

To set one or more options, place them after the chunk name, separated by commas. Try setting one or more options in the following chunk:
```{r code chunk options}
2+2

hist(rnorm(1000))
```

You can execute a code chunk by clicking the green triangle button in the top-right corner of the chunk.

## Basic formatting

### Paragraph breaks and forced line breaks

To insert a break between paragraphs, include a single completely blank line.

To force a line break without starting a new paragraph, put two blank  
spaces at the end of a line.


### Headers

You can create a header by placing one or more `#`s at the beginning of a line followed by a blank space. The number of `#`s indicates the size of the header — i.e., whether it is a section, sub-section, sub-sub-section, etc.

### Bulleted and numbered lists

- Item 1
    - Item 1a, created by indenting two spaces (or more) or a tab before the `-`.
      - Item 1a-1, you can keep nesting deeper with further indentation.
- Item 2
* Item 3 (`-` and `*` accomplish the same thing)

1. First step
    a. Sub-step
2. Second step
3. Third step



### Math

Some of your homework assignments this semester will include mathematical derivations in addition to computational/programming questions. You can use the same commands as you would in LaTeX to type math in R Markdown.

As an example, let's type out the first few steps of the solution to the ordinary least squares (OLS) problem. In simple linear regression, we want to find $\alpha$ and $\beta$ which minimize $\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i = 1}^n (y_i - \alpha - \beta x_i)^2$. To do so, we differentiate the objective function with respect to $\alpha$:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial}{\partial \alpha} \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i = 1}^n (y_i - \alpha - \beta x_i)^2 &= \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i = 1}^n \frac{\partial}{\partial \alpha} (y_i - \alpha - \beta x_i)^2 \\
&= \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i = 1}^n -2(y_i - \alpha - \beta x_i).
\end{aligned}
$$



### Tables

If you want to include a table in an R Markdown document, I recommend using an [online table generator](https://www.tablesgenerator.com/markdown_tables).

A sample table is below:

| Column 1   |      Column 2      |  Column 3 |
|----------|:-------------:|------:|
| col 1 is |  left-aligned | $1600 |
| col 2 is |    centered   |$12 |
| col 3 is | right-aligned |$1 |



### Images

You can include an image in an R Markdown document by using the following syntax:

`![Caption](/path/to/file/on/your/computer/image.jpg){width=...}`

If you prefer to write and scan your answers to non-programming homework questions, this is an easy way to include them in your final document.

![Example image](img1.jpeg){width=50%}


### Links

You can include a link in an R Markdown document by using the syntax `[text](link)`. For example, [here](https://rmarkdown.rstudio.com/lesson-1.html) is a link to an R Markdown tutorial.

# R fundamentals

## Vectors

```{r}
x <- c(1, 2, 3)
y <- c(4, 5, 6)

4 * x

x^2

x + y

x * y

x %*% y

x %*% t(y)
```



## Matrices

```{r}
mat1 <- matrix(data = 1:9, nrow = 3, ncol = 3)
mat2 <- matrix(data = -4:4, nrow = 3, ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)

4 * mat1

t(mat1)

mat1 %*% mat2
```



## Lists

A list in R is a flexible container that can hold different types of objects: vectors, matrices, numbers, or even text.

```{r}
my_list <- list(First_class = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 4, 4), 
                Second_class = matrix(1:4, 2, 2),
                last_element = 2.4,
                words = c("i", "love", "statistics"))

my_list$First_class

names(my_list)
```



## Data frames

A data frame is essentially a list of vectors. Each column of a data frame must have entries of the same data type. Different columns must have the same number of rows, but they can be of different data types. 

You can think of a data frame as a table

```{r}
# creating a data frame from a matrix
df1 <- data.frame(mat1)
df1

# creating a data frame column by column
df2 <- data.frame(col1 = 24:26, col2 = c("a", "b", "c"), col3 = c(4.5, 1.4, 5.1))
df2

# dimensions and column names
dim(df2)
colnames(df2)

# indexing rows
df2[1,]

# indexing columns
df2[,1]
df2$col1
```

Real datasets are typically stored and loaded in as data frames:
```{r}
str(iris)
```



## Conditionals (if/else)

```{r}
number <- 31

if (number > 30 & number < 31) {
  print("condition 1 satsfied")
}

if (number > 30 | number < 31) {
  print("condition 2 satisfied")
}

if (number <= 20) {
  print("less than twenty")
} else if (number <= 30) {
  print("less than thirty")
} else {
  print("less than forty")
}

ifelse(number <= 20, "less than twenty", ifelse(number <= 30, "less than thirty", "less than forty"))
```



## Loops (for/while)

```{r}
for(i in 1:5){
  print(i)
}
```

```{r}
i = 0
while(i < 5){
  i = i + 1
  print(i)
}
```

It's often more efficient to use `apply` functions instead of loops:
```{r}
# ?apply # `?` followed by the function name will open the documentation for the function
# ?sapply
sapply(1:5, function(i) {i ^ 2})
```

These functions are particularly useful when applying a function to all columns of a data frame:
```{r}
df1
sapply(df1, mean)
```



## Basic statistical functions

The following functions (and many others) are automatically available when you open an R Studio window.

```{r}
a <- iris$Sepal.Length
b <- iris$Sepal.Width

mean(a)

var(a)

cov(a, b)

cor(a, b)

sd(a)

median(a)

quantile(a, c(0.025, 0.975))

range(a)

min(a)

max(a)
```



## User-defined functions

```{r}
my_function <- function(x, y, z = 8) {
  if (!is.numeric(x) | !is.numeric(y)) {
    return("bad input(s): x and y need to be numeric")
  }
  
  result <- x + 2*y + z^2 - 3
  
  return(result)
}

my_function(x = 4, y = -12, z = 8)
my_function(x = 4, y = -12) # unless overridden, z = 8 by default

my_function(x = "stats", y = -12, z = 2)
```

It's actually not necessary to name a function. You can create a lambda function (AKA anonymous function) as follows:
```{r}
(function(x, y, z = 8) {return(x + 2*y + z^2 - 3)})(x = 4, y = -12)
```



## Packages

To use functions and datasets from packages that are not automatically installed by R, you'll have to install and load them as follows:
```{r}
# install.packages("tidyverse")
library(tidyverse)
```



## Plots

There are several built-in plotting functions in R.

Scatter plots:
```{r}
# ?plot
plot(x = iris$Sepal.Length, y = iris$Sepal.Width,
     col = iris$Species, pch = 19, cex = 1.5,
     xlab = "Sepal length", ylab = "Sepal width")
```

Histograms:
```{r}
# ?hist
hist(iris$Petal.Length, breaks = 40, col = "lightgoldenrod2",
     xlab = "Petal length", ylab = "Number of flowers")
```

Box plots:
```{r}
# ?boxplot
boxplot(iris$Petal.Width, horizontal = TRUE,
        col = "steelblue3", xlab = "Petal width")
```

However, I recommend using [`ggplot2`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/), which is a plotting package that provides more plot types and customization options. We'll learn more about `ggplot2` sometime in the next few weeks so that you can use it for your final project if you want to.

# Monte Carlo methods

## Sampling from probability distributions

For many common distributions, the `stats` package (which is loaded automatically) implements probability density functions (PDFs), cumulative density functions (CDFs), quantile functions, and sampling functions.

|    Function   |       Description        |
| ------------: | :----------------------- | 
| `d<distr>(x)`  |   evaluate PDF at `x`    |
| `p<distr>(q)`  |   evaluate CDF at `q`    |
| `q<distr>(p)`  |  compute `p`th quantile  |
| `r<distr>(n)`  | generate `n` iid samples |

Here's a list of some common distribution names (i.e., `<distr>` in the above table):

- `unif` (uniform)
- `norm` (Gaussian)
- `binom` (binomial)
- `chisq` (chi-squared)
- `exp` (exponential)
- `f` (F)
- `pois` (Poisson)
- `t` (t)
- `beta` (beta)
- `gamma` (gamma)
- `lnorm` (log-normal)
- `cauchy` (Cauchy)



## Setting the seed

Anytime you perform a random operation in R (e.g., sampling from one of the distributions above), you should set the seed to ensure that your results are reproducible.

```{r seed}
set.seed(451)
rnorm(5)

set.seed(269387)
rnorm(5)

set.seed(451)
rnorm(5)
```
